# Dleto Design

**Chisels** $\chi$ the name given to the sets $P$ of polynomials given to T and Z sets when P is an ideal generated by linear polynomials.  It is left unsaid if this should be the name for general situations.  Since T and Z sets depend only on the ideal generated by P any generating set for P will suffice as chisel but some generating sets are better computationaly than others.  When the ideal is generated by linear polynomials we can give it by a matrix of its coefficients and put that matrix in row-reduced echelon form.  Also since we can often rescale the weights of a derivation formula we can rescale the columns by a torus element (diagonal invertible matrix) and that further simplifies.  The matrices that have integer coefficients are most useful as they apply in all coefficients.  See `null_patterns.pdf`

**Derivation** or $\chi$-derivation, is the special name given to terms of the Z set elements when using a chisel P, i.e. a linear polynomial constraint.

**Densor**, a portmanteau of "derivation tensor" is the T set of a P chisel.

## Design

Use `ITensor` Julia library to keep up with the best in tensor algorithms for things like tensor contraction and reshaping functors.  However, those assume floating point numbers so there is a future hope to have an integer and finite field aware alternative.  In particular I want to expose the terms we regulary use

- **axes** an enumerable set $A$
- **base** an entropic algebra $\Delta$, e.g. a vector space for now to be the codomain.  In Julia by default vector spaces are array types so we just need the domain as real (some Julia float) or complex.
- **frame** a function $U:A\to Module$, evaluated $U_a$, that assigns to each axis its module or vector space in the field case.  In ITensors this is played by Index because it just needs the name of hte axis and the dimension of that vector space.  For long term modules would be needed and that needs a presentation not just a rank.  so a generalized index is long term needed.
-  **tensor space** is a module/vector space 
- **interpretation** the distributive function on the tensor space and frame into the base.  This is what actually caries out the contractions and it should do so on subsets of the axes as labeled.  
- **tensor** element of a tensor space.

- Should we include a dual space marker?  Frequently in tensor worlds duality and co-variant axes are important.  This would be a partition on A and the base would be handled as covariant.
_ I believe interpretation maps should include things like $U\to \hom(V,W)$ as well as $U\otimes V\to W$ because frankly they are equivalent in theory but in practice they force one to needlessly alter data.  



### T, I, Z sets

Each of T, I and Z depends on 3 parameters.  I will work only in the chisel case.

- $T_{\mathbb{T}}(\chi,\Delta)$ where $\mathbb{T}$ is a tensor space with axes $F=A\cup \{base\}$, P a set of polynomials indexed by $F$ and $\Delta$ is a subset of linear operators $(\omega_a:U_a\to U_a)_{a\in F}$.  The tensor space restriction is for example to insist solutions are symmetric tensors or some such thing.
- $Z_{\Omega}(T,\chi)$ $\Omega$ the space of operators, in the linear case over fields this can be reduced to things like who is engaged, whether the operators are symmetric, orthogonal, etc.  See paper.

Both T and Z use the same set up but they solve for different parts. For example, in 2 enaged axes $XM=NY$ gives you tensors $M$ and $N$ and solves for $X$ $Y$ to get $Z$-set elements.  In densor case we are given various $X,Y$'s aand want $M,N$ with $XM=NY$.  In trivalent form $XB+BY+B^Z=0$ solving ofr $(X,Y,Z)$ is a Z-set, solving for $B$ is a dnesor.  But any thoguhtful data structure for one likely helps the other.  

Users should be able to use fast linear algebra to solve.  I'd like to modularize that hcoise by having a Solver factory that lets you select and users choose but get defaults.
